title: Buying a Used Van: What the MOT History Tells You That the Advert Does Not
desc: How to read a van MOT history before you buy: the mileage trail, the advisories that actually matter on a working van, the gaps sellers never mention, and what a free check cannot tell you.
body:
The short version
  • A van that has done 90,000 honest miles is usually a better buy than one showing 45,000 with a patchy MOT trail.
  • Vans wear differently to cars. Look for suspension, brakes and corrosion advisories, not engine faults.
  • Most vans need their first MOT at three years, the same as a car. Vehicles used to carry passengers for hire or reward are the exception.
  • A gap in the MOT record is the single biggest thing an advert will never mention. It usually means the van sat unused or was off the road being repaired.
  • Every check on this page is free and takes about two minutes with the registration.

Why an MOT trail says more about a van than a car

A used car is mostly bought by one person who drove it to work. A used van has usually been a tool, and tools get used hard. That changes what you should be looking for in the record.

Vans carry weight. Weight destroys suspension, brakes and tyres long before it troubles an engine. So when you read a van MOT history, the interesting failures are almost never dramatic. They are the same boring components appearing again and again, which tells you the vehicle has spent its life loaded.

The other difference is mileage. A van doing 25,000 miles a year on motorways is in better mechanical shape than one doing 8,000 miles a year of stop-start urban delivery work, even though the second one looks better in the advert. Motorway miles are gentle. Multi-drop miles are not.

You can see all of this for free. Put the registration into the MOT history checker and read the trail rather than the headline.

Read the mileage trail first, before anything else

Every MOT records the odometer reading. Lined up in order, those readings are a chart of how the van has actually been used, and they are very hard to fake because they were recorded by different testers at different garages on different dates.

Three things to look for:

What you seeWhat it usually means
Steady 15,000 to 30,000 miles a yearNormal working van. Nothing to worry about.
A year with almost no milesThe van sat. Ask why. Long standing is hard on brakes, tyres, seals and batteries.
A reading lower than the one before itStop. Either a clerical error at the garage or the odometer has been wound back. Ask the seller to explain it in writing before you go any further.
A large jump then a sudden drop to very low annual mileageOften a change of use, for example a courier van sold on to a private owner. Not a problem in itself, but the hard miles are already in the vehicle.

Clocking is a real and profitable crime, and vans are a favourite target because high mileage hits van values hard. Our guide on how to spot a clocked vehicle goes through the full method, and it applies identically to vans.

The advisories that matter on a van

An advisory is the tester telling you something is wearing but has not yet failed. On a van, a repeated advisory is more useful than a one-off failure, because it shows a pattern the seller has ignored.

  • Corrosion, especially underneath. The most expensive words in a van MOT history. Look for corrosion noted on the subframe, sills, suspension mounting points or brake pipes. Once corrosion is structural, the repair bill can exceed the value of the van.
  • Suspension and springs. Repeated advisories here mean the van has been run loaded, often overloaded. Expect more of the same.
  • Brake pipes and hoses. Cheap to fix now, an MOT failure later, and a safety issue in between.
  • Play in steering or wheel bearings. Normal wear on a working van, but note how often it recurs.
  • Oil leaks noted as slight. Watch whether the same leak is still slight three years later or has been upgraded to a failure.

What matters far less than people think: a bulb, a wiper blade, a number plate lamp, or a single tyre below the limit. Those are consumables and they tell you nothing about the vehicle.

If you want the full breakdown of what actually causes failures and roughly what each one costs to put right, read what actually fails an MOT in the UK.

Gaps in the record, and what they hide

This is the check almost nobody does, and it is the one that finds the problems.

Lay the test dates out in order. An MOT lasts twelve months, so the tests should be roughly a year apart. If there is a gap of eighteen months, two years or more, the van was not being used on the road during that time. That is not automatically bad, but there are only a few explanations:

  1. It was declared off the road because the owner did not need it. Common with seasonal trades and second vans.
  2. It was being repaired after an accident or a major mechanical failure.
  3. It failed and was left until someone decided whether it was worth fixing.
  4. It was in a compound after being written off, then repaired and put back on the road.

Numbers three and four are the ones you care about. A free MOT history will not tell you which of the four it was. It will tell you that a gap exists, so you can ask the seller a specific question instead of a general one. "Why is there no MOT between March 2023 and October 2024" is a much better question than "has it had any accidents".

The free checks to run before you view

All of these take a registration number and no money.

CheckWhat it tells youWhere
MOT history and mileage trailUse, condition pattern, gaps, clocking riskOur free checker
Tax status and MOT expiryWhether it is road legal todayGOV.UK vehicle enquiry
Clean air zone and ULEZ liabilityWhether it costs you a daily charge to drive into a cityOur ULEZ checker
RecallsOutstanding safety recalls not yet carried outGOV.UK vehicle recalls

ULEZ matters more for vans than for cars. A pre-Euro 6 diesel van is charged daily in London and in a growing number of clean air zones, and for a working vehicle that can be hundreds of pounds a month. Check it before you buy, not after. You can compare two vehicles side by side if you are choosing between them.

What a free check cannot tell you

Be clear about the limits, because plenty of sites blur them.

A free MOT history check shows tests, mileage, failures and advisories. It does not show outstanding finance, whether the vehicle has been written off by an insurer, whether it is recorded as stolen, or whether it has been scrapped or exported. Those come from finance houses, the insurance industry register and the police, and no free service has them.

For a cheap van bought privately, an MOT history plus a careful inspection covers most of the risk. For anything expensive, or anything bought from a stranger with a story, a paid vehicle history check is worth the money. That is a genuine gap in what we currently offer for free, and we would rather say so than pretend otherwise.

The verdict

Read the mileage trail, count the gaps, and look for the same advisory repeating. A van with high miles, a complete record and boring consumable advisories is a better buy than a low mileage van with a two year hole in its history and fresh paint underneath. The record is free, it is official, and the seller cannot edit it.

title: What an MOT Actually Costs in 2026, and When the Retest Is Free
desc: The legal maximum MOT fee is 54.85 pounds for a car and 29.65 for a motorcycle, unchanged since 2010. What garages really charge, the free retest rules, and five ways to pay less.
body:
The short version
  • The legal maximum for a car MOT is £54.85. It has not changed since April 2010.
  • Motorcycles are capped at £29.65. Most garages charge well under both caps.
  • Typical real-world price is £30 to £45 for a car, and promotional deals from about £20.
  • From 6 July 2026 the caps rose for heavy vehicles: £70 for HGVs, £50 for trailers, £90 for buses and coaches.
  • A retest is often free. Whether it is depends entirely on where the vehicle went after it failed.

The legal maximum, and why nobody charges it

DVSA sets a maximum MOT fee by vehicle class. A garage may charge less. It may not charge more.

VehicleMaximum fee
Car, up to 8 passenger seats (class 4)£54.85
Motorcycle over 200cc (class 4 motorcycle)£29.65
Motorcycle up to 200cc£29.65 or less depending on class
Goods vehicle up to 3,000kg (class 7)£58.60
HGV, from 6 July 2026£70.00
Trailer, from 6 July 2026£50.00
Bus or coach, from 6 July 2026£90.00

Caps as published by DVSA and current in August 2026. The car and motorcycle figures have been frozen since April 2010.

Here is the part that matters. Almost no garage charges the cap. The MOT itself is barely profitable at any price; garages want the repair work that follows. So the test is used as a loss leader, and a typical honest price in 2026 is somewhere between £30 and £45. Chains and fast-fit centres run £20 to £25 offers regularly.

If you are quoted £54.85, you are being charged the absolute maximum by a garage that has decided you will not shop around. Ring two more.

When a retest is free, and when it is not

This is the rule that costs people the most money because it is not obvious and nobody explains it at the counter.

  • Leave the vehicle at the test centre and have the repair done there. If it is retested before the end of the next working day, the retest is normally free.
  • Take the vehicle away and bring it back within 10 working days. You get a partial retest, free for a specified list of items. This covers most common failures.
  • Bring it back after 10 working days, or with a failure outside the partial list, and you pay for a full test again.

So the expensive mistake is failing on a Friday, leaving the car on the drive for three weeks, then paying twice. If you cannot fix it quickly, at least get it back inside the ten working days.

Ask the question before you hand over the keys: "if it fails and I repair it myself, is the retest free within ten working days?" A garage that hesitates is telling you something.

Five ways to pay less, and one to ignore

  1. Book at a council test centre if you have one nearby. Some local authority sites test but do not repair, so they have no incentive to find work. This removes the conflict of interest entirely.
  2. Ask for MOT only, no service. Bundled deals often hide a service you did not need.
  3. Book in the quiet months. March and September are the busiest because of plate changes, and prices firm up. January and February are quiet.
  4. Fix the obvious things yourself first. Bulbs, wipers, screenwash, tyre pressures and a number plate light. Lighting is the single biggest failure category in Great Britain and most of it is a bulb.
  5. Test early. You can test up to a month minus a day before expiry and keep the original expiry date, which gives you time to fix a failure without the car being off the road illegally.

What to ignore: pre-MOT checks sold as a separate paid service by the same garage doing the MOT. You are paying twice to be told the same thing.

The cost that is not the test

The test fee is the small number. The repairs are the big one, and the MOT history tells you what is coming before you pay for anything.

Put the registration into our free MOT history checker and read the advisories from the last two tests. An advisory is the tester saying a component is wearing but has not failed yet. The same advisory appearing twice is a failure being scheduled for you.

Our guide on what actually fails an MOT goes through the categories and rough repair costs, and the defect categories explains the difference between dangerous, major and minor.

Driving without one

Driving without a valid MOT can bring a fine of up to £1,000. If the vehicle is in a dangerous condition it rises to up to £2,500, three penalty points and a possible disqualification. Your insurance may also be affected.

There are two legal exceptions: driving to a pre-booked MOT test, and driving to a garage for repairs needed for the test. Both need to be genuine, and "I was on my way to book one" is not one of them.

Full detail in the MOT rules and fines guide.

The verdict

The cap is £54.85 for a car and £29.65 for a bike, and you should almost never pay it. Ring three garages, ask about the free retest window before you book, fix the bulbs yourself, and spend the difference on the advisories the last test already warned you about.

title: Every UK Clean Air Zone in 2026: Who Pays, How Much, and Where Cars Are Exempt
desc: Seven charging zones in England plus London ULEZ. Only three charge private cars. The full table, the Euro standards that decide it, and why Scotland works completely differently.
body:
The short version
  • England has seven charging clean air zones in 2026: Birmingham, Bath, Bristol, Bradford, Portsmouth, Sheffield and Tyneside, plus London ULEZ separately.
  • Only Birmingham, Bristol and London charge private cars. In Bath, Bradford, Portsmouth and Tyneside a compliant or non-compliant car pays nothing.
  • Vans and taxis are charged in far more places than cars are. If you drive a diesel van, this matters to you and not to your neighbour with the same age car.
  • Scotland works differently: Glasgow, Edinburgh, Aberdeen and Dundee operate bans with penalty charges, not daily fees.
  • The test is almost always Euro 6 for diesel, Euro 4 for petrol. Check your own vehicle free on our ULEZ and clean air zone checker.

Every charging zone in England, and who pays

Clean air zones come in classes, and the class decides which vehicles are charged. That is why two cities can both have a zone and only one of them charges you.

ZoneClassCars charged?Typical daily charge
BirminghamDYes£8 cars, taxis, private hire and vans. £50 HGVs, coaches and buses.
BristolDYesAll non-compliant vehicle types charged.
BathCNoCars and motorcycles exempt. Vans, taxis, minibuses, coaches, buses and HGVs charged.
BradfordCNoPrivate cars exempt. Most other vehicles charged.
SheffieldCNoCars exempt. Taxis, vans and buses charged.
Tyneside (Newcastle and Gateshead)CNoCars exempt. Most commercial vehicles charged.
PortsmouthBNoOnly non-compliant taxis, buses, coaches and HGVs. Cars and light goods vehicles not charged.

Positions as at August 2026. Zones are set by individual councils and can change, so confirm with the council before travelling if the charge would be significant.

London is separate and stricter. ULEZ covers all London boroughs and charges non-compliant cars, vans and motorcycles daily. The Congestion Charge is a different scheme again, in a smaller central area, and you can be liable for both on the same day.

What actually makes a vehicle compliant

The threshold is the emissions standard, not the age on the logbook, though age is a good proxy.

FuelStandard neededRoughly means
Petrol car or vanEuro 4Registered from about January 2006
Diesel car or vanEuro 6Registered from about September 2015
MotorcycleEuro 3Registered from about July 2007
Electric or hydrogenExemptAny age

Two things people get wrong. First, a diesel is judged far more harshly than a petrol, so a 2014 diesel is non-compliant while a 2007 petrol is fine. Second, these are guides, not guarantees. A vehicle registered close to the cut-off may or may not meet the standard depending on the exact engine. Check the registration rather than assuming.

Vehicles over 40 years old are generally exempt as historic vehicles, and there are local exemptions and discounts in most zones for residents, blue badge holders and some commercial operators. Those are set locally and you have to apply.

Scotland is a ban, not a charge

This catches people out badly, because the money involved is much larger.

Glasgow, Edinburgh, Aberdeen and Dundee run low emission zones. A non-compliant vehicle is not charged a daily fee. It is prohibited from entering, and if it does, a penalty charge applies. The penalty starts at a set amount and doubles for each repeat offence within a period, up to a capped maximum.

So an English driver who is used to paying £8 and thinking nothing of it can take a diesel into Glasgow and get a penalty instead. There is no "pay to enter" option. Check before you drive north.

Why this hits vans hardest

Look back at the table. In four of the seven English zones a private car pays nothing while a van pays. That is deliberate: commercial vehicles do more miles in city centres and older diesel vans are among the dirtiest things on the road.

For a working van this stops being a curiosity and becomes a real operating cost. A tradesperson driving into Birmingham five days a week in a pre-2015 diesel van is looking at roughly £40 a week, about £2,000 a year, purely to keep working the same patch.

That number should change what you buy. Our guide on buying a used van covers the rest of the checks, but on emissions the rule is simple: for a diesel van used in cities, Euro 6 is not a nice-to-have.

How to check yours in about a minute

  1. Put the registration into our free ULEZ and clean air zone checker. It tells you the likely compliance position from the vehicle record.
  2. If it is borderline, confirm with the operator of the specific zone. Every zone has its own official checker and theirs is the one that decides.
  3. If you are buying, check before you buy. A non-compliant diesel is cheaper for a reason, and that reason will be charged to you daily.
  4. Check the MOT history at the same time. It costs nothing and it is the other half of the same decision.

The verdict

If you drive a petrol car from 2006 or later, or any diesel from late 2015, you are almost certainly fine everywhere in England. If you drive a diesel van, you are the vehicle these schemes were designed around and you should check every city you work in. And if you are heading to Scotland, remember that there is no daily charge to pay, only a penalty to avoid.

title: Category A, B, S and N Explained: What a Written-Off Car Really Means
desc: A write-off is an insurance decision, not a mechanical verdict. What each category means, which can never be driven again, what it does to value and insurance, and how to find out.
body:
The short version
  • A write-off is an insurance decision, not a mechanical verdict. Plenty of written-off cars are structurally fine.
  • Category A and B can never legally return to the road. If someone is selling you one as a runner, walk away and report it.
  • Category S means structural damage was repaired. Category N means non-structural. Both can be sold and driven legally.
  • Expect a Cat S or N car to be worth roughly 20% to 40% less than the same car with clean history, and expect some insurers to decline it.
  • A free MOT history will not tell you a vehicle was written off. That data comes from the insurance industry register and needs a paid check.

What a write-off actually is

When a vehicle is damaged, the insurer compares the repair cost against the vehicle value. If repairing it does not make commercial sense, they write it off, pay the owner and take ownership of the wreck.

That is an economic judgement about one vehicle at one moment. A ten year old car with £2,500 of damage is written off. The same damage to a two year old car is repaired. So "written off" tells you the repair was uneconomic for the insurer, not that the car is unsafe.

Where it becomes your problem is that the wreck is then sold at salvage, repaired by someone, and put back on the market. Sometimes that is done properly. Sometimes it is not.

The four categories

CategoryWhat it meansCan it be driven again?
AScrap only. The entire vehicle must be crushed, including every part.Never. Nothing may be salvaged.
BBreak for parts. The body shell must be crushed, but parts may be reused.Never as a vehicle. Parts only.
S (was Cat C)Structural damage that was repairable. Chassis, crumple zones, suspension mounts.Yes, once repaired.
N (was Cat D)Non-structural damage. Cosmetics, electrics, trim, water damage, sometimes theft recovery.Yes, once repaired.

The S and N categories replaced C and D in October 2017. Older records may still show C and D, which map roughly to S and N respectively.

If a car is advertised as Category A or B and is being driven, something is seriously wrong. Either the seller is lying about the category or the vehicle should not exist. There is no legitimate version of that transaction.

Cat S and Cat N in practice

These are the two you will actually encounter, and they are not equivalent.

Category N is often minor. A stolen and recovered car with a smashed window and a ripped-out ignition can be Cat N. So can a car with flood damage to the interior, which is a very different proposition. The category alone does not distinguish between them, which is exactly why you need to ask what the damage was.

Category S means the structure was damaged. Done properly, on a jig, by a competent body shop, a Cat S repair can be sound. Done badly, the car will never track straight, will eat tyres, and will not protect you properly in another impact. You cannot tell which you are looking at from photographs.

What to ask for, in writing:

  • What was the damage, and where?
  • Who repaired it, and is there an invoice?
  • Was it repaired on a jig, and is there an alignment printout?
  • Has it had an independent inspection since?

A seller who has genuinely had a proper repair done keeps the paperwork, because it is the only thing that protects the value. A seller with no paperwork is asking you to take the risk they were not willing to document.

What it does to the money

  • Value. Expect roughly 20% to 40% below a clean equivalent, more for Cat S than Cat N, and more on desirable cars where buyers have choices.
  • Resale. The category stays with the vehicle for life. You will face the same discount when you sell, and a smaller pool of buyers.
  • Insurance. Some insurers decline recorded write-offs outright. Others load the premium. Get a quote before you buy, not after.
  • Finance. Many lenders will not finance a Cat S or N vehicle, which shrinks the buyer pool again.

None of that makes it a bad buy. A properly repaired Cat N car at 30% off, bought to keep for years, can be excellent value. It is a bad buy if you paid a clean-history price, or if you need to sell it in eighteen months.

How you find out, honestly

This is where we have to be straight with you about the limits of a free check.

An MOT history will not tell you a vehicle was written off. Our checker is free and it shows every test, mileage reading and advisory since 2005, which is genuinely useful and catches a lot. But write-off records come from the insurance industry register, finance records come from lenders, and stolen markers come from the police. None of that is public data and no free service has it.

What the MOT history can do is give you a reason to look harder:

  • A gap of a year or more between tests is consistent with a vehicle sitting in a compound and then being repaired. It has innocent explanations too, but it is worth a direct question.
  • A sudden change in advisory pattern, for example steering or suspension alignment issues appearing after a quiet history.
  • A test at a garage a long way from the previous ones, which can indicate the vehicle moved through the salvage trade.

Start with the free MOT history check and read the clocking guide while you are there, because the same trail answers both questions. If the car is expensive, or the history has a gap you do not like, pay for a full vehicle history check before you hand over money. On a £8,000 car it is the cheapest insurance you will ever buy.

The verdict

Category A and B are not road vehicles and never will be. Category S and N are legitimate buys at the right price with the right paperwork, and expensive mistakes without it. Ask what the damage was, ask who repaired it, get an insurance quote before you commit, and never pay clean-history money for a recorded write-off.

title: Lorry and Trailer Annual Tests: The 3,500kg Line That Decides Whether Your Van Gets an MOT or an HGV Test
desc: When a van stops getting an ordinary MOT and starts getting a DVSA annual test, the 2026 fees for lorries and trailers, the electric van exception that runs to 4,250kg, and the 14 day retest window that is worth real money.
body:
The short version
  • At 3,500kg design gross weight a van stops getting an ordinary MOT and starts getting a DVSA annual test. The cost roughly triples and the first test comes two years earlier.
  • The exception almost nobody quotes: a zero emission goods vehicle stays on the ordinary MOT up to 4,250kg. Same size van, electric instead of diesel, and you stay in the cheap lane.
  • Lorries, buses, coaches and trailers are tested every year from year one. Cars, vans and motorcycles get their first MOT at three years.
  • Retest inside 14 days and you pay a fraction of the fee. Day 15 and you pay the whole thing again.
  • Trailers are tested in their own right, with their own record, whatever is towing them.

The 3,500kg line, and what happens when you cross it

Most people running a van never think about this until they upsize. The moment the design gross weight goes past 3,500kg, the vehicle leaves the MOT system that cars, vans and motorcycles sit in and joins the annual test system that lorries, buses and trailers sit in. Different fee, different timetable, different place, different paperwork.

Here is the whole picture in one table. All figures are the GOV.UK maximum MOT fees and the DVSA annual test fees at authorised testing facilities, the latter last updated on 15 July 2026.

VehicleTestFirst test dueFee
Motorcycle, any engine sizeMOT class 1 or 23 years£29.65
Car, up to 8 seatsMOT class 43 years£54.85
Goods vehicle up to 3,000kgMOT class 43 years£54.85
Goods vehicle over 3,000kg up to 3,500kg, petrol, diesel or hybridMOT class 73 years£58.60
Zero emission goods vehicle 3,501kg to 4,250kgMOT class 73 years£58.60
HGV, 2 axlesDVSA annual test12 months£91
HGV, 3 axlesDVSA annual test12 months£113
HGV, 4 or more axlesDVSA annual test12 months£137

Read the two bold rows against the row above them. A 3,500kg diesel Luton pays £58.60 once every year, and nothing at all for its first three years. A 3,600kg diesel version of the same vehicle is an HGV: £91 a year, starting twelve months after it was first registered with DVLA. An electric 4,250kg version pays £58.60 and waits three years.

That zero emission threshold exists because a battery pack is heavy, and without it every electric van would have been pushed into the HGV regime by its own batteries. If you are running a small fleet and weighing up diesel against electric, this belongs in the sums alongside the clean air zone charges, because it moves in the same direction.

The real cost, including the fee nobody quotes

The £91 is not what you pay. Annual tests are carried out by DVSA assessors, but usually at a private site called an authorised testing facility, and the ATF is allowed to charge you separately for the use of its pit. GOV.UK caps that service charge:

Vehicle typeMaximum ATF service charge
HGV£70
Trailer£50

So a two axle lorry can cost £161 at the gate rather than £91, and a two axle trailer £104 rather than £54. That is the number to budget against. The ATF may charge two service charges if a dangerous goods test and an MOT happen in the same visit.

Trailer test fees at an ATF, for comparison:

TrailerAnnual testRetest within 14 daysAverage test length
1 axle£41£1820 minutes
2 axles£54£2525 minutes
3 axles£64£3330 minutes
4 axles£64£3335 minutes
5 axles£64£3340 minutes

Notice that the fee stops rising after three axles but the test gets longer. If you are booking a five axle trailer, book the slot generously.

The 14 day rule is worth real money

This is the single most actionable thing in the fee tables, and it is not signposted anywhere obvious.

If your vehicle fails and you bring it back within 14 days, you pay a reduced retest fee. Bring it back on day 15 or later and you pay the full annual test fee all over again.

VehicleFull testRetest within 14 daysRetest after 14 daysYou lose
HGV, 2 axles£91£35£91£56
HGV, 3 axles£113£49£113£64
HGV, 4 or more axles£137£65£137£72
Trailer, 2 axles£54£25£54£29

There is also a part-paid retest, £13 for an HGV and £7 for a trailer, which covers the narrow case where only a small part of the test has to be repeated.

Miss the window on a four axle unit and a trailer in the same week and you have thrown away roughly £100 for no reason other than scheduling. If a vehicle fails on a Friday, the repair booking matters more than the repair itself.

Prohibitions, which are not the same as a failure

A failed annual test is a planned, budgeted event. A prohibition is not.

DVSA and the police can carry out roadside spot checks, and where they find something serious enough they can issue a prohibition, which stops the vehicle being driven until the fault is put right. Clearing it needs a separate inspection, and that carries its own fee depending on how serious the fault was.

The practical point for anyone buying a used lorry, van or trailer: a clean annual test record is a snapshot taken once a year at a booked appointment, with the operator knowing the date months in advance. It tells you the vehicle can be got through a test. It does not tell you what state it is in on an ordinary Tuesday.

Where the records live, and what you can see for free

Good news, and it surprises people: the free DVSA MOT history service covers heavy vehicles too, not just cars and motorcycles. GOV.UK lists "check the MOT history of a vehicle" as one of the services under its own HGV, bus and trailer testing section, with records going back to 2005.

That means you can put a lorry or trailer registration into our free MOT history checker and get the same thing you would get for a car: the test dates, the results, the reasons for failure and the advisories. For a trailer this matters more than people expect, because a trailer is tested in its own right and carries its own record regardless of what has been towing it. Buy a tidy looking trailer with a bad history and you have bought the history.

What to read for, in order:

  • Gaps in the annual test dates. A heavy vehicle should be tested every year without exception. A missing year means it was off the road, and on a working vehicle that is unusual enough to ask about.
  • Repeat failures on the same item. Brakes and suspension appearing year after year say the vehicle is being patched to a pass rather than maintained.
  • Corrosion advisories. On a trailer chassis these are the expensive ones.
  • Mileage that does not fit the work. The same reading logic applies as on any vehicle. Our guide on reading a used van MOT history covers the method, and it scales up.

If you are choosing between two vehicles you can compare their records side by side before you travel to see either of them. And if you want the general background on what causes failures across all classes, what actually fails an MOT in the UK is the place to start.

The verdict

If you are running vehicles under 3,500kg, none of this applies to you and you do not need to do anything. Your van gets an ordinary MOT at three years and £58.60 a year after that.

If you are about to cross that line, do three sums before you sign. Add the ATF service charge to the headline test fee, because that is the real annual cost. Put every test date in the diary with a repair slot already blocked out inside 14 days, because that window is worth £56 to £72 per failure. And if the vehicle you actually need is a large van rather than a lorry, check whether the electric version keeps you under the 4,250kg zero emission threshold, because staying in class 7 is worth more than the test fee difference alone once clean air zones are counted.

The test record itself is free to read for every one of these vehicles. Read it before you buy, not after.
